documents.title: Memorandum: Natalie Panetti to Bob Derby re Martha Hamilton maternity/sick leave request
documents.subject: Internal memo about The Post's position on combining maternity leave with sick leave benefits under the Guild Contract, in relation to Martha Hamilton's request
documents.notes: Clean typescript memo; handwritten '7' at top left and page number '16' at top right. Names mentioned: Bob Derby, Natalie Panetti, Martha Hamilton, Larry Wallace, Jack Pierce.

pages.transcript:
[handwritten: 7]  [top right, handwritten: 16]

MEMORANDUM

                                                            May 4, 1976

FOR:  Bob Derby

FROM:  Natalie Panetti

RE:  Martha Hamilton - Maternity Leave/Sick Leave Request


This is evidently not a new issue. I've attached a copy
of the Guild Contract (Page 34, 4a and 4b) language
regarding Maternity Leave. Also attached is page 29 &
30 regarding Sick Leave (Article X as referred to in 4b).
This is definitely confusing.

Larry Wallace is out till Thursday, but I was able to
talk to Jack Pierce. According to Jack, The Post has
taken the position that:

1)  If a person, prior to the birth of a child and while
    still an active employee, becomes ill for any reason,
    she may avail herself of any sick leave benefits due
    her.

2)  Once an employee goes on leave for maternity reasons
    she is no longer eligible for sick leave--until she
    again becomes an active employee.

3)  In actuality, according to Jack, an employee is
    eligible for six months leave of absence for maternity
    reasons. The four weeks is strictly a guide to deter-
    mine the dollar amount an eligible person might receive
    as a maternity benefit.


bh

Attachments

documents.title: Confidential settlement document — salary/experience comparisons (Crenshaw, Faiola, Farhi)
documents.subject: Section of a confidential settlement-preparation narrative comparing the salary histories of colleagues (Crenshaw, Anthony Faiola, Paul Farhi) to Hamilton's and Mayer's at The Post/Financial News
documents.notes: Top and bottom of page cut off slightly ('Crenshaw' section begins mid-document, 'Paul Farhi' section continues past the page bottom). Header banner: 'CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES'.

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Crenshaw received four merit increases - two of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these two merit increases in 1994 and 1997.

Explanation:
Crenshaw (while having worked at The Post for almost an identical time period as Hamilton) had more journalism experience before coming to The Post (and also a higher prior salary). Therefore, Crenshaw was paid a higher starting salary than Hamilton. When Mayer started at The Post, Crenshaw was paid substantially more than Mayer at that time.

Crenshaw held a number of different editorial positions in National, Financial News and Real Estate for some 15 years. He retained his editor's salary when he became a reporter in Financial News.

He is considered an expert in tax and insurance issues.

Anthony Faiola

Anthony Faiola was paid less than Mayer on the 1995 and 1996 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Faiola came to The Post in the mid-1990s as a reporter in Financial News. He left Financial News in 1997 to become a Foreign Correspondent in the South America Bureau. Prior to starting at The Post, Faiola worked for four years as a writer/reporter at The Miami Herald. Faiola is a graduate of Florida International University with a degree in Journalism.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Faiola received approximately a 34 percent increase over his prior salary at The Miami Herald. His starting salary was less than the salary of Mayer at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Faiola received 12 merit increases - three of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these three merit increases in 1995 and 1996.

Paul Farhi

Paul Farhi was paid slightly more than Hamilton on the 1992 salary snapshot and more than Hamilton on the 1993 to 1998 salary snapshots. Farhi was paid more [page continues]
